text: In 1954 psychologist Leon Festinger's team joined a Chicago group awaiting a world-ending flood on December 21. When it failed, some members sought converts harder; later archives have cast doubt on parts of the account.

William Miller's followers expected Christ's return on October 22, 1844, and many gave away property. The "Great Disappointment" that followed gave rise to groups that later formed the Seventh-day Adventist Church.

Every February 15, followers of the John Frum movement on Tanna, Vanuatu, raise the American flag in honor of John Frum, a figure many link to the American troops who arrived with abundant goods in World War II.

The term "cargo cult" first appeared in print in November 1945, in a Pacific Islands Monthly article by a colonial resident of New Guinea. Many anthropologists now treat it as a dismissive label for complex movements.

In 1856 the young Xhosa prophet Nongqawuse said that if the people killed their cattle, the dead would rise and the British would be swept away. About 400,000 cattle were killed, and tens of thousands starved.
After failing the imperial exams four times, Hong Xiuquan came to believe he was Jesus's younger brother. His Taiping Heavenly Kingdom (1851–1864) fought one of history's deadliest civil wars.

Simeon Stylites, a 5th-century Syrian monk, spent about 37 years living on a platform atop a pillar near Aleppo. Crowds came to hear him preach, and he inspired generations of pillar-dwelling "stylites".

Some Japanese Buddhist monks practiced sokushinbutsu: years of a severely restricted diet, then burial alive while meditating, aiming to become a living Buddha. Only about 20 such mummies are known, many in Yamagata.

In 13th-century France, villagers near Lyon venerated Guinefort, a greyhound said to have been killed by mistake after saving a baby from a snake. A friar condemned the cult around 1250; visits went on into the 1940s.

Saint Christopher was never "de-sainted". The Catholic calendar reform of 1969 to 1970 left his feast to local calendars, mainly because it was a late addition to the Roman calendar, but he remains a recognized saint.

John Calvin joked in 1543 that the True Cross fragments in Europe would fill a ship. In 1870 the French architect Charles Rohault de Fleury measured the known relics and found they came to only a fraction of one cross.

By Sri Lankan tradition, a tooth of the Buddha reached the island in the 4th century, hidden in a princess's hair. For centuries whoever held it was seen as the rightful ruler; it now rests in a temple in Kandy.

The body of Saint Bernadette of Lourdes lies in a glass reliquary in Nevers, France, and is often called incorrupt. Its face and hands are covered with wax, added after a 1925 exhumation found the skin discolored.

Parsis in Mumbai traditionally leave their dead on Towers of Silence for vultures. After the cattle drug diclofenac wiped out most of India's vultures, the community installed solar reflectors to speed decomposition.

In Madagascar's famadihana, "the turning of the bones", families open their tomb every five to seven years, rewrap their ancestors in fresh shrouds, and dance with them to live music before returning them to the tomb.

The last known dated hieroglyphic inscription was carved at the temple of Isis on Philae in 394 CE. Procopius says Justinian had the temple closed around 537, though its priesthood may have died out decades earlier.

Plutarch tells how, under Tiberius, an Egyptian pilot named Thamus heard a voice from the island of Paxi tell him to announce that "Great Pan is dead". Christian writers later read it as the passing of the pagan gods.

The Donation of Constantine, a document claiming the emperor handed the popes rule over the western empire, was exposed in 1440 by Lorenzo Valla, who showed that its Latin could not date from Constantine's time.

Erasmus left the Trinitarian verse 1 John 5:7 out of his 1516 Greek New Testament because no Greek manuscript had it. He added it in 1522, after a Greek copy surfaced that had probably been written around 1520.

In 2012 a Harvard scholar announced a papyrus scrap in which Jesus speaks of "my wife". In 2016 a journalist showed that its provenance papers were fabricated, and the scholar agreed it was likely a forgery.

The Rigveda praises soma, a sacred drink pressed from a plant, in more than a hundred hymns, yet no one knows what the plant was. In 1968 R. Gordon Wasson proposed the fly agaric mushroom; ephedra is another candidate.

The Eleusinian Mysteries ran for centuries, and revealing them was punishable by death. One of the few hints to survive, from the Christian writer Hippolytus, says initiates were shown an ear of grain reaped in silence.

After Japan banned Christianity in 1614, hidden Christians kept their faith in secret for over 250 years, chanting prayers called orasho (from Latin oratio) and praying to Mary disguised as the Buddhist figure Kannon.
The Druze faith has accepted no converts since about 1043, when its period of open preaching, known as "the call", was declared closed. One can only be born Druze.
Cao Dai, a Vietnamese religion founded in 1926, counts among its Three Saints the Chinese revolutionary Sun Yat-sen, the Vietnamese poet Nguyễn Bỉnh Khiêm, and the French novelist Victor Hugo.

The Shakers, a celibate Christian sect, could grow only by conversion and adoption. In 2025 a new member joined their last community, at Sabbathday Lake in Maine, bringing worldwide membership to three.

In 1945 Egyptian farmers near Nag Hammadi dug up a jar of papyrus books holding the only complete Gospel of Thomas. By one finder's account, his mother burned some of the pages as kindling for the oven.

Around 144 CE the Christian teacher Marcion, expelled by the church in Rome, assembled the earliest known New Testament canon: one gospel (a shorter Luke) and ten letters of Paul, with no Hebrew scriptures.

The Oneida Community in New York (1848–1881) practiced "complex marriage", in which every member counted as married to every other. When it dissolved it became a company, Oneida Limited, famous for silverware.
At Cao'an, a small temple near Quanzhou in China, a stone figure carved in 1339 shows Mani, the 3rd-century Persian founder of Manichaeism, as the "Buddha of Light", with long hair and a beard.
